# Your First Cast-Iron Skillet Starts Here

**The 10-inch cast-iron skillet: seasoned, sturdy, and easier to care for than you've heard.**

Maybe you've heard that cast iron is fussy. The truth is that the routine is short: wash it by hand, dry it right away, and wipe on a little oil. That's it. In return, you get a pan that sears steaks, crisps potatoes, bakes cornbread, and moves from your stovetop into the oven. This skillet comes pre-seasoned with vegetable oil, so you can start cooking the day it arrives.

**$48**

**[Add to Cart]**

---

## Why You'll Reach for It Every Day

**Ready to cook from day one**
It comes pre-seasoned with vegetable oil, so you don't have to season it yourself before your first meal. Every time you cook and care for it, that seasoning keeps building.

**A real 10-inch cooking surface**
The flat cooking surface measures 10 inches across, with room for a couple of chicken thighs, a batch of eggs, or a skillet of fried rice. The rim measures 12 inches, so plan your storage space and lid size around that larger number.

**Heft that works for you**
At 6 pounds, this skillet is substantial. That weight makes it feel steady on the burner and helps it handle serious searing.

**Two handles for a confident grip**
A long handle steers the pan on the stove. A helper handle on the opposite side gives your second hand something to hold, which matters when you're lifting a full, heavy skillet in or out of the oven. Both handles are cast iron.

**Pour without the mess**
Two pour spouts, one on each side, let you drain pan drippings or pour off sauce from either side, whichever hand you use.

**Works on your stove**
It's suitable for gas, electric, ceramic, and induction stovetops.

**From stovetop to oven**
It's oven-safe to 500°F. You can sear a pork chop on the burner and finish it in the oven, or bake a pan pizza, skillet cookie, or cornbread.

## Care in Three Simple Steps

Cast iron care takes about as long as drying a regular dish.

1. **Hand-wash.** Clean the skillet by hand after cooking. Do not put it in the dishwasher. It is not dishwasher-safe.
2. **Dry immediately.** Don't let it air-dry or soak. Towel it off right after washing.
3. **Lightly oil.** Wipe a thin layer of oil over the surface before you put it away.

Follow these steps after every use and your skillet will be ready for the next meal.

---

## Good to Know Before You Cook

- **The handles get hot.** Both handles are cast iron, so they heat up along with the pan. Always use oven mitts to hold either handle, on the stovetop and when you take the skillet out of the oven.
- **It's 6 pounds.** Use both handles when you lift it, especially when it's full.
- **No lid in the box.** A lid is not included. When you choose one, measure it against the 12-inch rim diameter.

---

It's pre-seasoned and ready for your stovetop and oven. Your routine is wash, dry, oil.

# The Pan That Gives You a Golden Crust on Night One

**The 10-inch cast-iron skillet: 6 pounds of steady heat that does the hard part of searing for you.**

Here's what goes wrong for most new cooks. You lay chicken in a pan, it hisses for a second, then goes quiet and starts to turn pale and wet. A thin pan loses its heat the moment cold food lands in it.

This skillet is built to keep its heat. At 6 pounds of cast iron, it holds onto the heat you give it, so the sizzle keeps going and the outside of your food turns deep golden brown. You don't need chef skills. You need a hot, heavy pan and a little patience, and this is the pan.

It comes pre-seasoned with vegetable oil, so it's ready to cook the day it arrives. Afterward, wash it by hand, dry it right away, and wipe on a little oil.

## Your First Sear, Step by Step

**1. Heat it longer than you think.**
Set it on the burner (gas, electric, ceramic, or induction) and give it several minutes. Cast iron heats gradually, but once it's hot, it stays hot.

**2. Add oil, then add your food.**
A thin layer of oil, then the chicken thigh, pork chop, or smashed burger. Listen for a loud, steady sizzle. The weight of the pan keeps that sound going.

**3. Don't touch it.**
This is the beginner secret. When food first hits the pan, it may grip the surface. Leave it alone. As the crust forms, it loosens, and you'll be able to flip it cleanly.

**4. Finish in the oven if it's thick.**
Thick chop or bone-in chicken? Move the whole skillet into the oven, which is safe up to 500°F, to cook it through without burning the outside. Grab both handles with oven mitts. They're cast iron and they get hot.

**5. Pour off the drippings.**
Tip the pan using whichever of the two spouts suits your hand, then use the drippings for a quick pan sauce or discard them.

---

## Why Beginners Do Better With It

**Mistakes are easy to recover from.**
There's no coating on this pan, just cast iron and seasoning. If the surface starts to look dull or dry, the fix is the same routine as always: wash by hand, dry right away, and wipe on a thin layer of oil. Every time you cook and care for it, the seasoning builds.

**Room to avoid crowding.**
The 10-inch cooking surface fits two or three chicken thighs with space between them. Crowding is the other big reason food steams instead of browns. (The rim is 12 inches across, so measure storage and any lid against that number. A lid is not included.)

**Steady on the burner.**
The 6-pound weight keeps the pan planted while you flip and stir. The helper handle gives your second hand a solid grip for lifting it full.

## Care in Three Simple Steps

Cast iron care takes about as long as drying a regular dish. You don't need special products. The oil is probably already in your pantry.

1. **Hand-wash.** Clean the skillet by hand after cooking. Do not put it in the dishwasher. It is not dishwasher-safe.
2. **Dry immediately.** Don't let it air-dry or soak. Towel it off right after washing.
3. **Lightly oil.** Pour about half a teaspoon of **vegetable oil or canola oil** onto a paper towel and wipe it over the cooking surface. Then take a clean paper towel and wipe again until the pan looks smooth and dark, not wet or shiny. A thin layer is all it needs.

**Which oil should I use?**
Use **vegetable oil**, the same oil this skillet was pre-seasoned with, or **canola oil**. Both are neutral, inexpensive, and easy to find. Keep a bottle next to the stove so step 3 takes ten seconds.

**Keeping the seasoning strong**
The seasoning on your skillet builds every time you cook with it and follow the routine above. If the surface ever looks dull, dry, or patchy, don't worry. That's normal, and you don't need a new pan. Wash it by hand, dry it right away, and wipe on a thin layer of vegetable or canola oil. Repeat after the next few uses, and the surface will darken and even out as you keep cooking.

**Too much oil?**
If the pan feels sticky or tacky, you used a little more oil than it needed. Wipe it firmly with a clean paper towel. Next time, use less.

Follow these steps after every use and your skillet will be ready for the next meal.
